sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage B
sections.intro: Weir Farm is a national park on the sixty-acre site of painter J. Alden Weir’s home in Connecticut. Read “Weir Farm” and answer questions 10–14. Vocabulary notes follow the poem.

lines.text: Not vistas, but a home-sized landscape,
beloved rooms storied, painted, lived.
A farm bought with a painting
and a ten dollar personal check.
And almost from the beginning,
the intention to pass on
what an artist sees, what artists make.
A parcel of land, a vast legacy.
Admire the houses, barns, outbuildings,
and studios, uniformly Venetian red.¹
Respect the visible sweat work of stones
laid in walls and foundations, terraces and walks.
Admire the sunken garden, the wildflower meadows,
the path through thick woods to the fishing pond.
Walk through the farm envisioned by artists.
Admire the home artists made.
Or you can step from a museum’s polished floor
across a carven,² gilded threshold
into the farm reimagined in brushstrokes.
From that wooden bridge over there,
hear those three women’s tinkling laughter?
Over there the other way, see
the black dog panting near the youngish man
lifting stones into a half-built wall?
Step out of the frame again, and be
enveloped in birdsong and dapple.³
Feel the welcome of small particulars:
the grove beside that boulder,
the white horse tied in front of that barn.
With eyes made tender, see
those elms, from shadows on the grass
to the highest leaves’ shimmer.
With your friends, lovers, family, stride
across this chromatic⁴ broken brushwork.
Sit a minute at the granite picnic table
with the artist’s daughters, dressed in summer white.
You can daub⁵ this earth, so lyric, so gentle,
from the limited palette of your own love right now.
Any place you care for can hold an easel.
Everything around you is beautiful plein air.⁶
¹ Venetian red — warm red
² carven — carved
³ dapple — spots of color or light
⁴ chromatic — colorful
⁵ daub — to apply paint with quick strokes
⁶ plein air — the act of painting outdoors

questions.prompt: The “intention” stated in line 6 most likely refers to Weir Farm serving to
questions.explanation: The poem says the farm passes on what artists see and create, then invites visitors to admire the farm and imagine its scenes as art. Its intended legacy is an appreciation of artistic vision.

choices.text: enjoyment felt by visitors to the farm
labor expended by builders of the farm

questions.explanation: “Visible sweat work” calls attention to the physical effort required to lay stones in walls, foundations, terraces, and walks. The lines emphasize builders' labor.

questions.prompt: Lines 17 through 19 imply that people who view a painting can

choices.text: imagine themselves as part of the artwork
imagine themselves as creators of the artwork

questions.explanation: The viewer is invited to step from the museum floor across a threshold “into the farm reimagined in brushstrokes.” That imaginative crossing places the viewer inside the scene depicted by the painting.

questions.prompt: The description in lines 33 through 35 asks people to take the time to
questions.explanation: The speaker asks visitors to stride with loved ones, then “Sit a minute” amid the farm's colorful scene. Pausing encourages them to notice and appreciate the beauty around them.

questions.prompt: The poem is primarily developed through the use of
questions.explanation: Descriptions of red buildings, stonework, gardens, birdsong, dappled light, a white horse, and shimmering leaves build vivid sensory scenes. Imagery is the poem's main method.
